newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bond yields up, nervous ahead of US data.
newsitem.headline: Australia bond yields up, nervous ahead of US data.

text.p: *Australian bond yields rose as the market became nervous ahead of this week's barrage of data, particularly out of the U.S., continuing last week's retracement from two-month lows.
*Local key data not due until second half of week.
Australian bond yields rose as the market became nervous ahead of this week's barrage of data, particularly out of the U.S., continuing last week's retracement from two-month lows.

"The market is getting concerned about the numbers in the U.S. this week. Given the amount the market has rallied in the past few weeks, it was probably due for a correction," said Christopher Bell, Director of Treasury at Dresdner Australia.
Computerised selling found the market long of stock, fuelling the weak tone triggered off by consecutive falls in U.S. Treasuries while the Australia was closed for ANZAC Day.
The U.S. first quarter employment cost index is due on Tuesday, one of several key indicators due out in a week which ends with the April non-farm payrolls report on Friday.
Signs of strength are likely to reinforce expectations that the Federal Open Market Committee will endorse a further tightening in Fed funds when it meets on May 20.

Locally, the market sees average weekly earnings and building approvals on Thursday, and retail trade data on Friday. "If they come out on the low side then you will get some more speculation of the potential of another rate cut again," said Stephen Roberts, chief economists at UBS Australia.
The market had started to build in the possibility of an easing in 6.0 percent official interest rates last week when the "living wage" case showed a modest outcome.
However, profit-taking amid some disappointment that last week's benign inflation report was not even better has seen some of that expectation eroded.
RBA deputy governor Stephen Grenville told a conference that he was confident that Australian inflation would remain low, but only through continuing viligance of monetary authorities.
However, traders said his comments had no impact.

The local market generally underperformed the dollar bloc, particularly the New Zealand short end which remains supported by a firm N.Z. TWI. Canadian debt was undermined by a weakening Canadian dollar on Friday and prior to Canadian PM Jean Chretien calling a June 2 general election on Sunday.
